title: Photography direction for a small clinic
metaTitle: Small clinic website photography of the real room
excerpt: Photograph the clinic room and the clinician who works in it. Stock smiles and procedure collages are not proof. The picture should be part of the reason to book.
alt: A person in a blue shirt signing a paper document with a pen, a specific task in frame, for photography that should show a real clinician at work rather than a posed smile.
caption: A person signing a paper. A clinic photo should be a real task in a real room. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should clinic photos show?
faqs.answer: Show the room a patient will enter and the clinician who will see them, doing the work or standing in that room. Include access facts if a picture can show them, such as a step at the door, and repeat the fact in text. Skip stock smiles, cash-register cheer, and close-ups of instruments meant to impress.

faqs.question: Are before-and-after photos a good homepage image?
faqs.answer: Not as the first thing an anxious patient sees. They over-promise, they can shock, and they often outrun what you are allowed to claim. If you are permitted to show a result, put it on a specific page with context and consent. The homepage should be the room, the person, and the booking.

faqs.question: How do we brief a photographer for a clinic?
faqs.answer: List the rooms, the people, and the tasks. Say what to refuse: models, handshakes, staged laughter, and procedures performed for the camera. Ask for quiet frames a patient could recognize on arrival. Caption each selected file the same day, while you still know which room it is.

markdown:
Small clinic website photography should show the room and the clinician. A patient who is already anxious treats pictures as a preview of the hour, not as decoration. Stock smiles and a procedure list, even as a collage, fail that preview.

The pictures are part of the argument. If the page says who will see them and where, the photograph should be that person and that place. A mood of "care" pasted under the headline is a costume.

## A preview of arrival

Decide what the patient is trying to preview. The door. The waiting chairs. The treatment room. The face of the clinician. Those are the frames. A fountain, a skyline, and a handshake do not answer the preview. They answer a brand exercise.

Google's guidance on helpful content talks about first-hand experience and about showing how something was done, including with photographs. A clinic site can meet that standard simply. Photograph your rooms this month, not a rental, not a hospital you do not work in. A patient who arrives and finds a different room will feel the site lied. That feeling is hard to repair in a gown.

Wabisabi, a public Hanabi project, is a calm visual world that stays specific about materials. The lesson for a clinic is the specificity, not the subject. Calm is right. Generic calm is not. A quiet photo of your actual chair is better than a loud photo of a model in a white coat.

Shoot at the time of day patients come, with the lights you actually use. A room blasted with studio flash will not match 9 a.m. in winter. The mismatch is what people notice when they are already scanning for danger. Faithful light is part of consent. You are asking them to trust a preview.

## The clinician, occupied or simply present

Photograph the people named on the about page, in the room where they see patients, with consent and with a right to refuse. Occupied is better than posed. Reading a note. Washing hands. Standing where they stand when they explain a plan. Laughter in a stairwell can be human and still be the wrong hero, because it does not show the visit.

Do not ask a clinician to mime a procedure they are not doing, on a person who is not a patient, for the sake of a dynamic frame. Staged procedures look like stock even when the faces are real. They also teach the patient to expect that procedure in a first visit. If your first visit is a conversation, photograph a conversation's geometry: two chairs, a little distance, the clinician's hands empty.

Name them in the caption. "Dr. Shah in the first-visit room" is a caption. "Our wonderful team" under four people is a dodge. If one person opted out of photos, do not crop a stranger in. Leave a gap and use type. Honesty about who is pictured is a clinical courtesy.

Update the files when people leave. A homepage portrait of a former clinician is a serious defect. Put a review of images on the same list as the roster. The camera roll is not an archive you can ignore because the pictures still "look professional."

## What to refuse

Write the refusals into the brief so they survive the shoot.

- Stock smiles and stock families.
- Models in white coats.
- Handshakes across a desk.
- Close-ups of needles, drills, or blades as a hero.
- Before-and-after pairs on the homepage.
- A wall of procedure names designed as a graphic.
- Children as props unless the clinic sees children and you have the right consent.
- A fake window view that hides a real basement, if you are in a basement. Show the basement and the light you have.

The swap test is simple. If the frame could sit on a clinic site in another city without change, it is not yours. Specific beats reassuring.

Also refuse pictures that contradict the copy. If the first visit has no procedure, do not lead with an instrument tray. If the entrance has steps, do not only photograph the accessible entrance you do not have. The picture is an argument. Make it the same argument as the sentence about access.

## Dignity, consent, and patients in frame

Default to no patients in marketing photos. The room and the staff are enough. If a patient wants to be included, get written consent that says where the image will appear and for how long, and avoid details that turn the image into a record of their condition. A marketing page is a poor place for a clinical image.

Do not photograph people in distress, even your real patients, even with permission you feel good about in the moment. Distress reads differently on a homepage a year later. The goal is a preview that lowers fear, not a document of fear.

Children, and anyone who cannot consent on their own, are out of the marketing set unless a guardian process and a real reason survive a second look a week later. When in doubt, leave them out. You can show a child-friendly corner of the room with no child in it.

Staff consent matters too. A clinician who agreed to a portrait did not agree to a cropped detail used as a metaphor on a paid ad. Say where files may go. Advertising is a different exposure than the about page. Separate the permissions.

## Crop, caption, and text that carries the fact

Crop to the proof. The door handle and the step, if the step is the fact. The two chairs, if the conversation is the fact. The clinician's face at a size that reads on a phone. A wide architectural shot that makes the person a speck is the wrong hero for a small clinic. People are booking a person.

WCAG 2, as the W3C describes it, treats images as content that still has to be perceivable. The four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A photograph that carries the meaning of the page, such as who works here, needs a text alternative that carries the same fact. Alt text should say what is in the frame. "Dr. Shah seated in a small treatment room with two chairs and a window." Do not stuff the alt with a keyword. Do not leave it as "IMG_2044."

The caption can add the decision. "This is the first-visit room. Procedures are not done in this visit." The alt describes. The caption interprets, briefly. The paragraph next to the image should still make sense if the image fails. Patients on slow phones, and patients using screen readers, get the preview in words or they do not get it at all.

Color should look like the room. Heavy teal grades and blown highlights make skin and walls false. False color is a small lie, and small lies accumulate on a health page. Hanabi's design tools include Figma and Illustrator for the layout around the photo, not for inventing a room you do not have.

## A shot list for one morning

You can shoot a small clinic in a morning if the list is strict.

1. The entrance, including the step or the lift, in daylight.
2. The waiting chairs, empty and real.
3. The first-visit room, wide enough to understand, tight enough to feel small if it is small.
4. The clinician in that room, not performing.
5. The desk, if the desk is part of the arrival, with the person who sits there if they agree.
6. One detail patients ask about: the bell, the payment point, the coat hook. Not an instrument tray unless the visit truly includes it.

Give the photographer the sentences from the homepage, not a mood board of other clinics. "Show the two steps and the bell" produces a useful frame. "Make it welcoming and premium" produces a smile and a plant.

Shoot the crops you will need. A phone hero, a portrait crop, a wider indoor frame. Do not rely on a single file to survive three cuts. The step at the door is the first thing a bad crop removes, and it may be the fact a patient needed most.

If the morning is all you can do, stop there. A handful of true frames will outlast a library of stock. You can add photos when a room changes. You should not launch on borrowed faces because the shoot was inconvenient.

## After you choose the frames

Select for recognition. Would a patient know they were in the right building? If the answer is no, the frame is pretty and unfinished. Reshoot that setup rather than covering it with a headline.

Store the chosen files with captions and consent notes beside the other brand files. On a Hanabi project that is the client portal, so the next page does not pull an outtake of a former staff member. Name files by room and person, not by "final-final."

Put the pictures into the phone layout and remove the text in your mind. Do you still know where you would sit and who you would see? If the images only say "clean" and "nice," they are not clinic photography yet. They are hospitality photography. Hospitality is pleasant. It is not the decision this patient is making.

Those frames have to survive a narrow screen, because that is where the preview usually happens. [The mobile visit for a small clinic](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-small-clinic) is about keeping the room, the clinician, and the booking intact when the page is a column.
